title: Tell HN: Remember to migrate away from .name domain
content:
Comments
If you have a third.level.name domain, it'll get permanently expunged next year. Have you successfully taken steps to migrate away? Did you move to a standard .com domain, or are you taking your chances with another .tld?

Personally, I'm stuck in Microsoft hell because Azure admin emails cannot be changed and support is both uncaring and powerless.

nikanj · Oct 14, 2026

In case you haven't heard about this, see https://domainnamewire.com/2026/09/03/third-level-dot-name/

jolmg · Oct 17, 2026

> His registrar informed him that his registration will be terminated in February (even though it’s paid through 2040).

Wonder if registrars will refund to people's cards.

cowlevel · Oct 17, 2026

Definitely not. No company ever refunds unless you sue them, they're worried you'll sue them, or they want a good reputation, and domain registries do not care about reputation because they are monopolies. Registrars might, a little, but it's not up to them.

toomuchtodo · Oct 14, 2026

Consider editing title to be "Tell HN:" Thank you for the PSA!

nikanj · Oct 14, 2026

Good point, changed. Thanks!

mindaslab · Oct 14, 2026

Why re they doing this? Looks stupid to me.

nikanj · Oct 14, 2026

By kicking old nerds off legacy.domain.name, they can relist domain.name on the open market and make an absolute killing.

cowlevel · Oct 17, 2026

This is the reason.

PufPufPuf · Oct 17, 2026

And they don't do refunds if you prepaid!

layer8 · Oct 17, 2026

If even only two people would be interested in foo.example.name and bar.example.name, they could make more of a killing with the old scheme. Apparently such interest is lacking.

kiesel · Oct 17, 2026

Worth noting, this doesn't affect domain.name, thus 2nd level domains. I was actually unaware you could directly register a 3rd level domain... Got my .name in the sunrise phase of .name, though it later rendered obsolete by name change on marriage (but still got it).

mnd999 · Oct 17, 2026

I have a second level and I’m in the process too. This kind of shitty behaviour warrants bankruptcy.

pelagicAustral · Oct 17, 2026

Biggest rug pull in the history of dns

InsidiousWombat · Oct 17, 2026

Nah, turning existing domains premium (sometimes 10x or higher cost) under the users is IMO worse, as it can catch people that just have it on auto-renew unaware.

hoppp · Oct 17, 2026

This. Happened to me a few times.

I get a cheap domain for allegedly $1 renew and then get charged for $10 because they changed their minds. It should be illegal.

zarzavat · Oct 17, 2026

See also: .eu revoking registrations of UK residents after Brexit.

moron4hire · Oct 17, 2026

Jesus Christ. In 25 years of working on the Web, this is the first time I'm hearing of "third level domains". WTF? Where and when did this come from?

No shade to the folks being harmed by this situation. Sorry. I'm just really non-plussed at the idea that the registrar is charging for what looks like should be a DNS prefix.

edent · Oct 17, 2026

You've never seen example.co.uk? Many countries use them because the top level domains for gov, edu, etc are restricted to one country.

dspillett · Oct 17, 2026

Those are not quite the same though, being something specific and short so essentially behave like a tld in their own right. For a long time you couldn't buy a <something>.uk, it had to be .co.uk or similar, so those _were_ the tld.

The way .name worked you could directly register <name1>.<name2>.name instead if getting <name2>.name and setting up <name1> as a subdomain. It meant john.smith.name and dave.smith.name could be completely separate registrations. You can't generally register <name1>.<name2>.tld like that.

Symbiote · Oct 17, 2026

There's two on the second page of active HN discussions, telegraph.co.uk and independent.co.uk.

Should we mention fourth-level domains, like ci.east-palo-alto.ca.us or stanborough.herts.sch.uk?

TZubiri · Oct 17, 2026

there’s nothing special about any level of domains, it was always a hierarchical protocol

jeroenhd · Oct 17, 2026

The difference is that .name allowed you to buy steven.smith.name and someone else could buy john.smith.name. The shared hierarchy between those names is the .name domain, .smith.name doesn't really exist.

Of course, this could be trivially fixed if .name would take the shared part of every second level domain, treated it like a TLD for legacy customers, and turn it into a hierarchical system.

But they'd need to do that for possibly thousands of paying customers, there's no way they'd be able to afford that, Verisign only makes 1770000000 dollars of yearly revenue! Honoring these existing contracts would bankrupt them!

jeroenhd · Oct 17, 2026

.name has been doing this for 25 years so I guess you must've missed them right when you got started!

For .uk, this scheme was the default until 2014 (a long time, considering it's first use was in 1985). Everything was .co.uk or .org.uk and you bought those directly with registrars. Then, in 2014, .uk registrations were allowed, and the .co.uk and .uk domains now coexist.

jl6 · Oct 17, 2026

It’s so ad hoc that we need to maintain reference datasets to identify what’s registrable:

https://publicsuffix.org/

A real mess.

victorbjorklund · Oct 17, 2026

Unrelated. What happened with .io? Didn’t they say they would disappear or did that change?

Symbiote · Oct 17, 2026

The proposed treaty between Britain and Mauritius was conditional on the approval of the USA (due to the UK/US air base), and that approval wasn't given.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Indian_Ocean_Territory

swiftcoder · Oct 17, 2026

That approval would likely have been considered a mere formality under other administrations, but unfortunately intersected with the current administration's obsession over territory...

wodenokoto · Oct 17, 2026

Wait, so if you own Johnson.name you and use John.Johnson.name as your web address, that will stop working?

OtomotO · Oct 17, 2026

I don't think so. If you own it, you can have any subdomain.

At least I hope this is the case. I have a memorial page for my uncle under hisfirstname.ourlastname.name

OJFord · Oct 17, 2026

No this is people who have registered john.johnson.name, but johnson.name remains Verisign's (and e.g. unrelated Alice has also registered alice.johnson.name)

PufPufPuf · Oct 17, 2026

Which is an insane scheme to begin with. Why not "john-johnson.name"?

OtomotO · Oct 17, 2026

tbh, as an owner of a .name (tld) I don't understand how this worked in the real world.

I have subdomains like {myfirstname}.{lastname}.name ... {lastname}.name is mine

So obviously {myfirstname}.{lastname}.name is a subdomain...

Could someone now have bought {myfirstname}.{lastname}.name and DNS would go to their page?

If so, I find the new behaviour way more sane...

If I wanted to sell a subdomain, I could do this, no questions asked. I just point the subdomain to another IP.

But I pay for {lastname}.name so it should be mine, just like any other .tld I have!

wakamoleguy · Oct 17, 2026

Yes, if you pay for {lastname}.name, the full domain is yours, including whatever you want to do with subdomains. However, .name also allowed direct registration of third level domains ({firstname}.{lastname}.name). These were mutually exclusive by domain… so if somebody registers the 3rd level, nobody can directly buy the 2nd level, and vise versa. As far as I understand, it was first come first serve based on the 2nd level domain.

There were also some shenanigans around automatic email routing in that case.

Meleagris · Oct 17, 2026

Ok. But why would anyone buy a third level domain when they could have bought the second level? It’s a strange thing.

Were the third level domains cheaper?

Me personally, it wouldn’t even occur to me to register a third level directly, because why bother when you can have the second level and do whatever you want with it.

Super strange.

Arrowmaster · Oct 17, 2026

When the TLD first opened up you were not allowed to purchase {lastname}.name, it was restricted to third level domains only in an attempt to lure in customers wanting {first name}@{lastname}.name as an email address. But they didn't make it easy to configure that email redirect if you used another registar than verisign, and email has evolved.

Later in a desperate search for MORE MONEY, they opened up 2nd level if no 3rd level already existed under that 2nd. This sounds less like another search for more money with new sales as people are saying, but a reduction in unique domain handling and cost cutting (they can shutdown all those email redirection servers).

Giorgi · Oct 17, 2026

Soo... people actually used it?

cpach · Oct 17, 2026

Not very many, but yes

BrandoElFollito · Oct 17, 2026

I had a .name domain since its birth. Then proceeded to loose it because of bad luck and bad planning.

I tried to retrieve it but after a week of back and forth exchanges (mostly back from my side) I gave up.

Moved to .fr hoping that it will be stable (price wise) as a national TLD - so far so good.

layer8 · Oct 17, 2026

National TLDs from major developed nations and .com/.net/.org are the only TLDs I would consider safe for the long-term.

(I’m excluding restricted-use TLDs like .edu here.)

gonzalohm · Oct 17, 2026

I'm not sure I get it. If anyone registers a domain first.second.name then you are basically registering a subdomain under second.name, right? You don't own anything, second.name owns your subdomain and can do whatever they want with it

bichiliad · Oct 17, 2026
